Topic: Calibration drift in uncertainty-aware classifiers deployed across shifting label ontologies

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-3296)
response:
Uncertainty-aware classifiers are models that output not just a predicted class but a distribution or score reflecting confidence — the central question here is whether those confidence scores remain calibrated (i.e., a stated 90% confidence actually corresponds to ~90% empirical accuracy) when the label ontology shifts: when categories are split, merged, deprecated, or redefined after deployment. The key concepts are calibration (typically measured by Expected Calibration Error or reliability diagrams), ontology drift (distinct from covariate/data drift — the meaning of labels changes, not just the input distribution), and the compounding problem that a model can appear accurate on old metrics while silently miscalibrating on the new semantic space. A beginner sees ontology change as a labeling bookkeeping problem; an expert worries that post-hoc calibration methods like temperature scaling or Platt scaling were fit to the original label structure, so their correction factors are now systematically wrong in ways that won't surface in aggregate accuracy numbers. The deeper trap is that uncertainty estimates tend to be most confidently wrong near the decision boundaries that ontology changes specifically disturb — the model has been trained to be certain precisely where the new ontology introduces ambiguity.

When a coarse label — say, "pneumonia" in a chest-X-ray classifier — is split into "bacterial pneumonia" and "viral pneumonia," the model's learned decision boundary reflects the original single-class statistics: it was trained to push representations of all pneumonia cases toward one region of the embedding space, away from "no finding" and "pleural effusion." The new fine-grained boundary must run through that region, but the model has no learned feature axis that reliably separates the two subtypes — so the split boundary lands in a zone where the model's softmax outputs are characteristically high-confidence for the original class. This is worse than noise: noise would mean confidence scores scatter randomly, but instead you get systematic overconfidence because the softmax geometry interprets "far from all other old classes" as "very certain," even though the point sits exactly on the new decision boundary that matters. Guo et al. (2017, "On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks") showed that deep networks are already overconfident post-softmax; ontology splitting selectively worsens this in the subregion where the old class was most coherent and the new distinction is most consequential. In NLP, Desai & Durrett (2020) found that calibration degrades most sharply on examples near class boundaries — splitting moves many previously "interior" examples to boundary status without the model's temperature or scaling parameters knowing this has happened. The practical consequence is that a downstream decision-maker (a radiologist using the confidence score as a triage threshold) receives the highest false confidence precisely on the cases that are now the hardest to distinguish.

The backbone contains sufficient separating information when the fine-grained classes are linearly separable — or nearly so — in the frozen embedding space; this is the implicit bet you're making when you retrain only the head. A clean way to test this before committing is to run a linear probe: fit a logistic regression on the backbone's penultimate-layer embeddings using a small labeled sample of the new fine-grained classes, and check both accuracy and the ECE of that probe. If linear probe accuracy is high but ECE is poor, the representations are discriminative but the geometry doesn't support calibrated probabilities — you'll need at minimum a calibration step (temperature scaling on the new classes) on top of head retraining. Kornblith et al. (2019, "Do Better ImageNet Models Transfer Better?") showed that linear separability of embeddings in the source task is strongly predictive of transfer accuracy, but critically this says nothing about calibration, which depends on how separated the clusters are (margin width, cluster compactness) not just whether a hyperplane exists. A more targeted diagnostic is to compute the Bhattacharyya distance or Mahalanobis distance between the embedding distributions of the two new fine-grained classes — if those distributions substantially overlap in the frozen space, head retraining will produce a boundary in a low-margin region where softmax confidence is structurally inflated. In medical imaging, Raghu et al. (2019, "Transfusion") found that for CheXNet-style chest X-ray models, shallow transfer (head-only) matched full fine-tuning on accuracy but the calibration gap was significant precisely for semantically similar classes — exactly the split-label scenario. The practical threshold: if linear probe accuracy on the new split falls below ~80% with reasonable data, the backbone is not encoding the relevant distinguishing features and freezing it will produce a confidently wrong head.

With borderline Bhattacharyya distance, the embedding distributions overlap in a fat middle region but have separable tails — so the classifier can reliably distinguish the easy examples (those in the well-separated tails) but produces a compressed, ambiguous softmax distribution for the overlapping core. On a reliability diagram, this produces a characteristic U-shaped calibration error across confidence bins: the low-confidence bins (0.5–0.65) are actually underconfident because the model hedges on the genuinely ambiguous overlap region, while the high-confidence bins (0.85–1.0) are overconfident because the model extrapolates the tail-separation geometry too aggressively to examples that are only moderately separated. This is structurally different from an undertrained backbone, where the calibration error tends to be monotonically overconfident across all bins — the model hasn't learned meaningful structure so softmax outputs cluster near the decision boundary but get pushed high by the temperature of a poorly-regularized training run, producing the classic overconfidence signature Guo et al. (2017) documented with ResNets on CIFAR. The diagnostic signature of borderline separation is therefore the crossover: underconfidence at middling scores, overconfidence at high scores, with a relatively well-calibrated narrow band around 0.7–0.8 where the model's uncertainty accidentally matches empirical frequency. In practice, tools like NetCal (Küppers et al., 2020) can bin-wise decompose ECE and reveal this U-shape, which is the fingerprint you'd present to justify partial fine-tuning of later backbone layers rather than head-only retraining — the backbone is encoding something useful but the representation geometry is warped in the overlap region in a way a new head alone cannot fix.

The core tool here is elastic weight consolidation (EWC, Kirkpatrick et al. 2017), which penalizes updates to weights that are high-importance for the original task as measured by the diagonal Fisher information matrix — in practice this means the fine-tuning loss has an additional term that resists moving weights the old task relied on most, preserving the embedding geometry that supports coarse-class calibration. A more calibration-specific approach is to maintain a held-out set of original-class examples and add a distillation term (Hinton et al. 2015) that forces the fine-tuned model's softmax outputs on those examples to stay close to the frozen backbone's outputs — this directly anchors probability scores rather than just weights, which is what you actually care about for calibration. The practical tension is that EWC's Fisher estimates are computed once at the original training time and become stale as fine-tuning proceeds, so a cheaper operational alternative is layer-wise learning rate decay: set the learning rate for early backbone layers at ~1/10th the rate for later layers, preventing catastrophic drift in low-level representations while allowing the high-level geometry to reshape. Santurkar et al. (2021) showed in the context of distribution shift that calibration on held-out domains degrades roughly proportionally to the L2 weight displacement from the original parameters, which gives you a concrete monitoring signal — track weight displacement per layer during fine-tuning and stop or reduce LR when displacement in early layers exceeds an empirically set threshold. In medical imaging deployments specifically, Mehrtash et al. (2020) found that joint training on old and new label sets with a calibration-aware loss (label smoothing set to reflect empirical class confusion rates) outperformed post-hoc recalibration alone for preserving multi-class ECE. The failure mode to watch is that all these methods protect accuracy on old classes reasonably well but calibration can quietly degrade even when accuracy holds — so the monitoring metric must be per-class ECE on the coarse classes, not aggregate accuracy.

The Fisher information matrix estimated on the original distribution measures how sensitively the original loss responds to weight perturbations under original data statistics — when fine-tuning data has a different covariate distribution, the Fisher entries for weights that mediate distribution-specific features become systematically wrong as importance proxies, either over-protecting weights that happen to be high-variance on the old data but irrelevant to the new task, or under-protecting weights that are low-variance on old data but critical for shared abstract features the new distribution also needs. Concretely, if the original training set was hospital-A chest X-rays and the fine-tuning split data comes from hospital-B with different acquisition protocols, the Fisher will over-weight scanner-specific texture filters (high variance on hospital-A data) and under-weight anatomy-encoding filters (lower variance but transferable) — so EWC will paradoxically freeze the wrong weights. Schwarz et al. (2018, "Progress & Compress") showed that Fisher-based importance estimates degrade as a function of distributional distance between tasks, and proposed online EWC with a running Kronecker-factored approximation (K-FAC Fisher) that partially mitigates this by continuously updating importance estimates — but this requires storing and updating a structured approximation to a matrix that scales with parameter count, which is expensive. A cleaner diagnostic is to compare the spectral overlap between the gradient covariance matrices of old and new data: if the top eigenvectors of the new-data gradient covariance are orthogonal to those of the old-data Fisher, the importance estimates are operating in essentially disjoint subspaces and EWC protection is nearly useless. In that regime, the more robust strategy is subspace-based methods like gradient projection (Saha et al. 2021, "Gradient Projection Memory"), which constrains fine-tuning updates to lie in the null space of the old task's gradient subspace regardless of per-weight importance scores — this is distribution-agnostic because it operates on gradient geometry rather than magnitude statistics. The practical implication is that Fisher-based EWC should be treated as unreliable by default when fine-tuning data is out-of-distribution relative to original training, and the burden of proof is on showing spectral alignment before trusting it as a regularizer.

When the new fine-grained classes require feature directions that fall outside the null space of the old gradient subspace, gradient projection silently truncates exactly the updates that would sharpen the new decision boundary — the model converges to a solution that minimizes old-task interference but cannot represent the discriminative axis the new split requires, producing a classifier that is confidently wrong in the overlap region because it has literally been prevented from learning the relevant geometry. The calibration failure is insidious: training loss on the new classes may appear to converge because the head adapts to whatever projected features are available, but the underlying representation is impoverished, so confidence scores in the ambiguous region are high (the head is doing its best with available signal) while empirical accuracy is low — the worst possible calibration signature. The detection test before deployment is to measure the alignment angle between the top-k gradient directions of the new fine-grained task and the null space of the old gradient subspace: if the new task's dominant gradient directions have large components within the old subspace (i.e., small projection residual), a large fraction of the useful update signal is being discarded. Concretely, compute the SVD of the old gradient covariance matrix to get the protected subspace basis U, then for a batch of new-task gradients g, measure ||g - UUᵀg||/||g|| — if this ratio is substantially below 1.0 (say, below 0.7), more than 30% of the new gradient signal survives projection, but if it's near 0.3, you're discarding 70% of the discriminative update and calibration will degrade proportionally. Saha et al. (2021) noted this failure mode but didn't quantify the calibration consequence; the closest empirical characterization comes from Farajtabar et al. (2020, "Orthogonal Gradient Descent") who showed task accuracy collapses when gradient overlap exceeds ~40% of explained variance. The production monitoring signal is to track the ratio of new-class ECE to new-class accuracy during fine-tuning: when projection is working, both improve together; when the null space is insufficient, accuracy plateaus early while ECE continues to worsen, because the head keeps adjusting confidence outputs without gaining real discriminative power.

The framing that makes this tractable is to convert asymmetric miscalibration costs into a constrained optimization: rather than minimizing a weighted sum of old and new ECE (which requires commensurable cost units you rarely have), you set a hard ECE budget on the old classes — derived from the downstream decision loss, e.g., "miscalibration on 'no finding' cannot increase by more than 0.02 ECE because that corresponds to X additional false discharges per 1000 patients" — and then maximize new-class calibration subject to that constraint. This maps onto a Pareto frontier problem where you sweep the protected subspace dimension (how many old-task gradient directions you retain) and measure the (old ECE, new ECE) operating point at each setting, then select the point on the frontier that satisfies the old-class budget — this sweep is cheap if done on a validation set before full fine-tuning commits. The asymmetry is encoded not in the optimization objective but in which side gets the hard constraint: in radiology triage, missing a "no finding" miscalibration is a liability event while imperfect bacterial/viral pneumonia confidence is a softer clinical cost, so the constraint is one-sided. Cen et al. (2023, "Partition-based Calibration") showed that class-conditional ECE budgets can be enforced during training via per-class temperature parameters updated with a Lagrangian penalty, which gives you a principled mechanism to implement the hard constraint dynamically rather than as a post-hoc recalibration step. The practical complication is that the cost asymmetry itself is often not quantified by the deploying organization — in that case, the operationally defensible move is to elicit it indirectly: ask stakeholders to specify the maximum tolerable false-positive rate change on old classes, convert that to an ECE bound using the existing reliability diagram, and use that as the constraint boundary. The failure mode to avoid is treating this as a hyperparameter tuning problem and picking the tradeoff that maximizes aggregate metrics — aggregate ECE will almost always favor sacrificing the minority new classes, which are typically the ones where miscalibration has the highest per-instance cost.
